::: {.why}
The test of an honest conclusion is whether its form depends on which way the result came out, and last night's exercise is the one that catches it.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State the phase's conclusion as a number with an interval and a stated comparison.
- Confirm the conclusion's wording does not depend on the direction of the result.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Write the verdict section of reports/milestone-07-ml.md: the comparison, the interval, the seed spread, the turnover, and the conditional analysis with its caveat. Then apply the correction for the phase's trial count from research_log.jsonl to the winning model.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Run the direction test: give the verdict to yourself with the sign flipped and check whether you would have written it the same way. Then write the paragraph on what you would need to see to change your conclusion, which is the section that makes the rest credible.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Note what the phase cost: hours spent against the improvement obtained, stated plainly. That ratio is a legitimate part of the conclusion.
:::
:::

## Resources

- [Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu (2014) — Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism](https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/backtest-pseudo.pdf) [paper]{.res-kind}
- [Harvey, Liu & Zhu (2014) — ...and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns](https://www.nber.org/papers/w20592) [paper]{.res-kind}

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
The verdict section written, direction-tested, with the trial-count correction applied and the effort-to-improvement ratio stated.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
State the phase's conclusion in one sentence with a number and an interval, then say what would change it.
:::
